passage:
Akash,

You're the only one I can say this to, so I'm writing it down.

On Sunday Papa said, in front of Mummy, that I was "wasting my degree in a call centre". I told him it hurt. He laughed and said, "I never said that. You're too sensitive, beta, you imagine things." Mummy looked at her plate.

This happens all the time. He says something, I react, and then it never happened. Last year it was about my wedding savings. Before that, about my college. I've started to wonder if I really do remember things wrong.

So I've begun keeping notes on my phone, date and exact words, right after. Reading them back, I'm not imagining it. I'm his daughter, not a liar.

I don't need Papa to agree. I just need to trust myself. And I needed one person to know.

Can we talk this weekend, just us?

Your sister,
Aditi

qa.a: He said she was "wasting my degree in a call centre".

qa.q: How does Aditi feel when Papa denies what he said?
qa.a: Aditi feels hurt and confused, starting to doubt her own memory.

qa.q: What steps is Aditi taking to trust herself?
qa.a: She keeps dated notes of exact words, trusts her own experience, and talks to her brother, without needing Papa to agree.

qa.q: How might Mummy be feeling when she looks at her plate?
qa.a: Mummy may feel uncomfortable and afraid to take sides, unwilling to contradict Papa.

grounding: A letter shows a young woman whose father denies what he said and calls her too sensitive, who keeps notes, trusts her experience and confides in a trusted person.

Vinita, you asked why I've started writing things down in that little green notebook. I'm Charu, and it's because of my mother.

For years, she would say something cutting, like "No wonder no one stays with you," and when I cried, she'd say, "I never said that. You make up stories to hurt me." Then my aunt would call and ask why I was upsetting her. I honestly started believing my memory was broken.

Last Diwali, she denied saying something my cousin had heard too. My cousin looked at me and said quietly, "She did say it, didi." I nearly cried from relief.

That's when I started the notebook. Date, words, who was there. Not to show her. Just for me, so I stop doubting myself.

I also talk to you, obviously. And I've booked a counsellor.

I know what happened. I don't need Amma to agree anymore.

qa.a: It is green.

qa.a: Charu felt huge relief, nearly crying, after years of doubting her own memory.

At lunch Abbu said, "Yash has been promoted again." Then, to Tanvir: "And you're still at the same small company?" The old burn rose in Tanvir's throat. He was twenty-six, and he felt twelve.

He went for a walk by the Gomti in the evening. He didn't want to pretend nothing had happened. He also didn't want to spend every visit at war.

So he decided: shorter visits, two days not five. He'd spend more time with Ammi, who had always tried. He'd stop hoping Abbu would change.

That night he looked up a counsellor near his flat in Pune and booked a call for the next week.

"You're barely eating," Nikita said, finding Jatin on the terrace of their parents' house in Rohtak.

"I can't sit at that table without remembering."

"The belt?"

He nodded. "And the way Papa laughed when I cried. Now he acts like we were a perfect family."

Nikita sat beside him. "I remember too. I just don't say it."

"That sounds fair."

"And my office has a counselling helpline. I think I'll call them."

Nikita squeezed his shoulder. "I'll come with you next Diwali. Same night. We leave together."

In their town near Satara, whatever went wrong in Divyansh's house was Divyansh's fault. When the buffalo fell sick, it was because he'd fed it late. When his younger brother fought at school, Divyansh should have been watching. By twenty-three he had stopped arguing. He just said sorry, automatically.

His friend Manoj, who taught at the village school, noticed. One evening at the tea stall, Divyansh apologised to the stall owner for a cup of tea that had gone cold on its own.

"Why are you sorry?" Manoj asked.

Divyansh laughed, then didn't. "Habit."

"You know it's not true, right? That it's all you?"

Divyansh stared at the road. Nobody had ever said that.

Over the next months, he started spending evenings at Manoj's, reading. He applied for a job at the sugar factory in the next town. When he moved there, the first thing he noticed was how quiet his head was.

qa.a: He apologised for a cup of tea that had gone cold on its own.

qa.a: Divyansh felt stunned and moved, since nobody had ever questioned the blame before.

qa.q: How did Divyansh begin to see himself more clearly?
qa.a: He built outside support with Manoj, spent evenings reading, and took a job in another town for some distance.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Divyansh's automatic apologies?

Sunday, after the family wedding.

Three aunts, four uncles, same question. "Karthik, how much are they paying you now?" "Simran's husband is in America, you know. And you, a grown man, still single?" Periamma even pinched my stomach. "Getting round, kanna."

By the time the rasam came, I felt about two feet tall.

But I tried something new this time. I'd practised in the car.

To the salary question: "Enough for your gift, Periappa!" Everyone laughed and moved on.

To the marriage question, to Chithi: "When it happens, you'll be the first to know." Firm smile. Changed the subject to her garden.

To the stomach pinch: "Please don't do that," quietly. She blinked. Stopped.

On the way home I realised something. Chithi's own son hasn't found a job in two years. These questions are their worries, not my worth.

I'm Karthik. I'm doing fine. That's enough.

passage:
Counselling note, session two. Client: Amandeep, 25, software engineer, recently moved from Amritsar to Bengaluru.

Amandeep said her family calls her every evening. Her mother cries on the phone; her uncle has told relatives she "abandoned her parents for money". Last week her father refused to speak to her on his birthday. She described feeling guilty all day and angry all night. "I send money, I call every day, and I'm still the villain."

Her cousin Vandana, who also moved away for work, has told her this is how it was for her too, for a year.

We discussed ways she can show love that fit her real life: a fixed video call three evenings a week, rather than daily; one visit home every two months; a family photo album she is making for her mother. We also discussed that she does not have to justify her job again in every call.

She left saying, "I can be their daughter and still live here." Next session in two weeks.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep move from?
qa.a: She moved from Amritsar to Bengaluru.

qa.q: How does Amandeep feel about her family's accusations?
qa.a: Amandeep feels guilty all day and angry all night, as though she is the villain.

qa.q: What ways of showing love did Amandeep and the counsellor discuss?
qa.a: A fixed video call three evenings a week, a visit every two months, and a photo album for her mother, while no longer justifying her job in every call.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's mother feel about the move?
qa.a: Her mother likely feels sad and left behind, which shows in her crying on the phone.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young woman whose family says she abandoned them by moving for work, who feels guilt and anger, shows love in ways she can and stays firm on her decision.

Amma called again today. "You chose him over us. Your father hasn't slept since the wedding." Then Appa took the phone and said nothing at all, just breathed, and handed it back.

It's been six months since I married Arun. Not the boy from Madurai they picked. Arun from Kochi, who makes me laugh and irons my kurtas better than I do. I'm Madhuri, their daughter still, and they talk as if I died.

I cried in the bathroom for an hour. Then I got angry. Then I felt guilty for being angry.

Rehana, my colleague, said, "Love them the way you can. Don't undo your life."

So here's what I'm doing. I'll keep calling every Sunday. I sent Amma the jasmine she likes from the market near our flat. I invited them for Pongal. I will not apologise for marrying Arun.

They may take time. Months, maybe. I can wait. I just won't go backwards.

passage:
Thursday night.

Swati aunty, Ammi's old neighbour from Bhiwandi, came for lunch today. When Ammi went to the kitchen, she told me something I never knew. At eleven, Ammi was already cleaning houses. Her father drank. She was hit if the floors weren't shiny.

I sat there with my tea going cold.

All my life Ammi has been sharp. If my dupatta was crooked, she'd slap the back of my head. If I cried, she'd say, "Stop your drama." I've been angry with her for years.

Tonight I'm not less angry exactly. I'm sad. For her at eleven, scrubbing someone's floor with nobody to protect her. It made me softer, somehow.

But understanding isn't excusing. When I have children, I'll never hit them. And with Ammi, I'll be kind, and still leave the room when she starts shouting.

I'm Zainab. I'm her daughter, and I don't have to become her.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after hearing Swati aunty's story?
qa.a: Zainab felt sad and softer toward Ammi, though not less hurt.

qa.q: How does Zainab hold compassion and boundaries together?
qa.a: She plans to be kind to Ammi but still leave the room when she shouts, and to never hit her own children.

qa.a: Swati aunty may have felt protective of Ammi and wanted Zainab to understand where her harshness came from.

"The Grewals are coming on Sunday," Yogesh said at dinner. "Their son is a doctor in Canada. It's decided."

Simran put her fork down. "Papa, nothing is decided. I haven't even met him."

"You're twenty-four. Your mother married at twenty."

"And I'm finishing my architecture license next year. I want to work first."

He was silent a long time. "Sunday they come for tea. Only tea. Nothing is fixed."

Simran breathed out. "Thank you, Papa."

I'm Kishore, the eldest son, and in our family that meant one thing: I would run Papa's hardware shop in Nashik and marry whoever Mummy chose. Nobody asked. It was just how things were.

But I wanted to teach. Physics, at a school. For two years I said nothing. I felt pinned between loving them and losing myself.

My younger sister Kashish was the first person I told. She said, "Bhaiya, you have to say it. And not by shouting."

So I did, on a Sunday, calmly. "Papa, I respect the shop. You built it from nothing. But I want to be a teacher." He went red. Mummy started crying.

Kashish spoke up: "He's good at it, Papa. He taught me all of Class 12 physics." Later Mama, Mummy's brother, sided with me too.

It took a year. Papa hired a manager. I teach at a school in Pune now. We still argue. But I never once called them backward, and I'm glad.

qa.q: Where was Papa's hardware shop?
qa.a: It was in Nashik.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel during the two years of saying nothing?
qa.a: Kishore felt pinned between loving his family and losing himself.

qa.q: What helped Kishore follow his own path without contempt?
qa.a: He explained calmly and respectfully, gathered allies in Kashish and his uncle, and never looked down on his parents.

qa.q: How might Kishore's father have felt hearing his son's choice?
qa.a: Papa probably felt hurt and angry, going red, since he had always assumed his son would take over the shop.

passage:
Wednesday.

It's been four months since I stopped answering Dad's calls. Manoj asked tonight if I miss him. I said no too quickly.

The truth is two things at once. I sleep better. I don't flinch when my phone rings. I don't spend Sundays bracing for his voice, the drunk voice that told me every week I was a useless son. Relief, every single day.

And then tonight a man at the bus stop had the same cough, and I had to walk away because my eyes were stinging. I'm grieving a dad I never really had.

I've been checking myself. Is this anger talking? I don't think so. I didn't cut him off after one bad fight. It was twenty years. My counsellor helped me decide it calmly, over months.

If he ever gets sober and gets help, maybe I'll open the door a crack. Only if it's safe.

I'm Thomas, and I'm allowed to have both feelings.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Thomas have about the estrangement?

Mehak, you ask why I don't push your uncle Harpreet to come to the family functions. Let your Amandeep bua tell you.

When I was twenty-five, my younger brother stopped speaking to me. No reason I could see. I was bewildered, and so hurt. I asked my mother, my cousins, even his friends, to tell him to call me. That only made it worse.

Then my cousin brought me a letter from him. It said that when our father died, I had taken over everything, the house, the decisions, even his wedding, and never once asked what he wanted. Reading it, I wanted to defend every choice.

That was my turning point. I didn't defend. I wrote back: "You're right. I took over. I'm sorry. I won't send anyone to you again. Whenever you're ready, I'm here."

Then I waited. Three years. One Lohri he came to the door with rewri. We talk now. Slowly.

His mother kept saying, "I'll talk to her." His aunt kept saying, "I'll make her call you." Nothing worked. The deadline made it worse; every day, Tarun felt more bewildered and more hurt.

Then his cousin said quietly, "She says you never listen. That you always decide what's right for her."

Tarun wanted to argue. He had only ever been trying to help! He stopped himself.

That night he asked his mother and aunt to stop pushing her. Then he wrote Ayesha a short message: "I'm sorry for how I've treated your choices. I didn't listen. I won't send anyone to you again. I'd love to be at your wedding, but only if you want me there."

passage:
I'm Alka, and my brother Lalit and I didn't speak for four years. It started with an argument about our mother's hospital bills and ended with both of us saying things we couldn't take back.

For years I waited for him to call first. He didn't. Neither did I.

Last month I saw a photo of his son's first birthday on a cousin's feed. A nephew I'd never held. Something in my chest cracked.

I wrote maybe fifteen drafts. The long ones explained everything, who said what, who was wrong. I deleted them all. The one I sent was four lines: "Lalit, I miss you. I'm sorry for what I said about Papa's money. I'd like to meet your son someday. No pressure."

He replied the next evening: "Me too. Sunday?"

We had chai. It was awkward. We didn't go over the whole fight. Since then, I've sent him a message every week. Small things. That's how it's coming back.

qa.q: How many years did Alka and Lalit not speak?
qa.a: They didn't speak for four years.

qa.q: What did Alka feel on seeing the photo of Lalit's son's birthday?
qa.a: Alka felt a crack of grief and longing for a brother and a nephew missed for so long.

qa.q: Why did Alka's short message work better than the long drafts?
qa.a: It was humble, owned Alka's part and asked for nothing big, avoiding a full accounting of the fight, so Lalit could say yes easily.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when he read Alka's message?
qa.a: Lalit likely felt relieved and moved, replying quickly that he missed Alka too.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone reaching out to a sibling after years of silence with a short, humble note, owning their part without demanding a full accounting, and rebuilding trust with small acts.

passage:
First Sunday of March. Omkar sat on his balcony in Nagpur with his phone. Three years since he and Ojas had stopped talking, after Omkar skipped Ojas's engagement over a work trip and then said something cruel when Ojas complained. He missed his little brother so much it felt like a stone in his stomach. He typed: "Ojas, I'm sorry I missed your engagement, and for what I said after. I was wrong. I miss you." He sent it before he could delete it.

Thursday. Ojas replied: "Thanks for saying it." Nothing more. Omkar felt a pang, but didn't push. He didn't ask Ojas to explain his side.

Three weeks later. Omkar had sent a message every few days: a photo of their old school, a cricket score, a birthday wish for Ojas's wife. On Saturday Ojas wrote: "Coming to Nagpur next month. Lunch?" Omkar read it standing up, grinning.

qa.q: What did Omkar skip that started the silence?
qa.a: He skipped Ojas's engagement over a work trip.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling on the balcony that first Sunday?
qa.a: Omkar felt a heavy longing and regret, missing his brother like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: How did Omkar rebuild trust after Ojas's short reply?
qa.a: He didn't push or demand Ojas's side, and kept sending small, steady messages until Ojas suggested lunch.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt reading Omkar's first message?
qa.a: Ojas may have felt cautious but touched, acknowledging the apology while still guarded.

grounding: The story shows a young man who reaches out to his brother after years of silence with a short, humble apology, owns his part without demanding an accounting, and rebuilds trust with small, steady acts.
